F I G U R E 1 Overview of data and analyses; (a) we assessed the accuracy of three proposed approaches to taxon-independent, DNA-based trait assignment on a unique, specimen-level dataset of COI barcodes and morphometric trait measurements. (b) reflective of a more feasible implementation of trait assignment in the near term, we also conduct a species-level analysis of the rates of Phylogenetic Assignment for some widely studied bee traits on a phylogeny constructed from publically available COI data. Note ‘queries’ in (a) refer only to specimenlevel data from collections reported herein at four sites; while ‘queries’ in (b) include both the specimen-level data and additional data of unidentified bee sequences from 17 other sites in China.

We built a specimen-level dataset of COI DNA barcodes and functional morphometric traits for comparing different approaches to DNA-based trait assignment. We used bee specimens and COI sequences from four locations in China (Figure S1); specimens were newly collected and sequenced at three locations, while those of Xishuangbanna were collected and sequenced earlier as described in (Liu et al., 2017). To collect a diverse set of bee species, we used blind sweep net and yellow pan traps around flowers (McCravy et al., 2019). Insect legs were stored in absolute ethanol and refrigerated until molecular work was conducted. The COI DNA barcode region (\~650 bp) was amplified; whole genomic DNA was extracted with DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kits (QIAGEN GmbH, Hilden, Germany) and COI amplified using several universal primer pairs. Polymerase chain reactions (PCR) were performed in $3 0 \mu \mathrm { L }$ solutions, following the protocol of (Hajibabaei et al., 2005) with minor adjustments (particularly, we extended annealing time to 1.5 min). Sequencing was conducted at Beijing Tianyi Huiyuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd, and quality was checked in MEGA v7.0 (Kumar et al., 2016).

methods for taxon-independent assignment of traits to query barcodes or metabarcodes via reference data, (i) Phylogenetic Assignment, (ii) Blast Neighbourhood and (iii) Blast Top Hit. For Phylogenetic Assignment, states of queries were predicted based on a Bayesian model of trait evolution built on a phylogeny (code available at [github.com/dchesters/barcodeFD](http://github.com/dchesters/barcodeFD)), with a single dependency, BayesTraits; (Pagel et al., 2004). In Bayesian modelling of trait evolution on a phylogeny, the rates of transition between states along the branches of the phylogeny are established based on known terminal states (herein, of the references), and then, the posterior probabilities of each state are predicted for unknown nodes (which include terminals, herein applied to ‘queries’). The Bayesian estimations were performed with 2,500,000 generations of MCMC simulations and sampling of every 2500 generations. Phylogenetic Assignment output was parsed with a Perl script (parse_bayestraits_tip_estimates.pl) with the initial 50% of generations discarded as burn-in.

Accuracy of each trait assignment method was assessed through leave-one-out (L1O) cross-validation (Yang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2012) on the specimen-level dataset. In each loop of L1O, the known state of a single individual (the ‘query’) is removed from the reference system (and thus the trait model in the case of Phylogenetic Assignment) and then predicted via each approach. This process is looped over all individuals (treating each as a query) and all available traits.

Assignment accuracy of the three approaches was statistically compared. To test whether there were complementarity and biases between tools, the family-level taxonomic diversity profiles were firstly compared according to the mean quantity of correct assignments of each family, and visualized in network diagrams using ‘network’ (Butts, 2008). Since the quantities of trait records with barcodes used as reference were different among various trait datasets, we considered rate rather than quantity to avoid biases in the metrics used to evaluate the efficiency of tools (Blast Neighbourhood, Phylogenetic Assignment and Blast Top Hit). For this, two different rates were evaluated: (1) correct assignment rate (proportion of correct assignments over all results); and (2) accuracy rate (proportion of correct assignments over all assignments).

Several factors are likely to affect the efficiency of trait assignment. To test whether the number of barcodes $( \mathsf { B } _ { \mathsf { N } } )$ affects performance, the correct assignment rate and $\mathsf { B } _ { \mathrm { N } }$ were evaluated by linear and nonlinear regression models in R ‘trendline’ (Mei & Yu, 2022). For the linear models, the data met the model assumption of a normal distribution, and for the nonlinear models, we used an asymptotic regression. The best-fit model was selected by evaluating the second-order AIC (AICc) and residual standard error (RSE) for small samples. To explore the relationship between the assignment rate and sequence similarities, we regressed the assigned states of each tool against the per cent identity to the nearest neighbour. The per cent identity to the nearest neighbour was the value inferred from the method Blast neighbourhood, which indicated sequences similarities. The assignment state (0: incorrect assignment; 1: correct assignment) was considered as the response value, and the similarity to the nearest neighbour was treated as a fixed effect. Different traits were used as random effect and logistic regressions (binomial response) with analyses performed with the R package ‘lme4’ (Bates et al., 2015). As a

A total of 2343 bees were newly collected from four sites, from which 1627 barcodes were generated: 237 from Beijing, 294 from Anhui, 742 from Yunnan and 354 from Jiangxi. From these collections, 8218 measurements were made over 1726 bee individuals as follows: Anhui (n = 121), Xishuangbanna (n = 512), Beijing

(n = 230), Jiangxi (n = 335) and museum specimens (n = 528) from various localities. We assessed three proposed approaches to trait assignment using the L1O strategy on newly generated specimenlevel trait records. The three tools showed biases for one of the five different bee families involved (Figure S6). Overall, both Phylogenetic Assignment and Blast Top Hit performed better than Blast Neighbourhood for Apidae and Halictidae, which are the two families with the most barcodes available, but this difference dis sipated for the other three families for which fewer barcodes were available. In the best-fit model for Blast Neighbourhood $( \Delta \mathrm { A l C c } . 0 5 \right.$ , Table S3), while the relationships of $\mathsf { B } _ { \mathrm { N } }$ to correct assignment rate were unclear for the other two tools (ΔAICc between linear and nonlinear model being .95) for the species-level analysis are given in Table 1.

F I G U R E 2 Comparison of assignment rates under low, median and high sequence similarities. Correct assignment rate (proportion of correct assignments over all results) for (a) Blast Neighbourhood; (b) Phylogenetic Assignment; (c) Blast Top Hit; accuracy rate (proportion of correct assignments over all assignments) for (d) Blast Neighbourhood; (e) Phylogenetic Assignment; and (f) Blast Top Hit. L = low similarity ( 94). denotes p ≤ .05, * denotes p ≤ .001, and ns denotes no significance based on t-test and Wilcox test. Circles indicate original data points.
![Image block](doc:13c0434/tier:advanced/page:9/block:5)

F I G U R E 4 Resultant trait prediction in the species-level analysis using Phylogenetic Assignment for an arbitrary segment of the bee phylogeny. The phylogeny comprises both named reference species and subject MOTU. Two traits shown: (a) intertegular distance, classed to quartiles, exemplifying a rather labile morphometric trait with (given the current distribution of known states) a low rate of confident predictions, and (b) sociality, a conservative life-history trait with relatively high rate of successful prediction. Tips of interest for each trait are symbolled; triangles denote tips with known states and circles denote MOTU subject to trait prediction, within which the pie chart proportions denote Bayesian trait probabilities. For each of the two traits, the legend gives states along with assigned colours, as used in pie charts.

Note: Query MOTU includes only those of ‘unestablished species’; sequences within species-level thresholds to references were not included; rates are thus conservative. ‘Queries predicted’ are the number of MOTU for which there is no information for given trait and thus subject to Phylogenetic Assignment. Likely, successful assignments are summed in ‘Trait state predictions with p > 95%’. Traits partitioned by F (Female), M (Male) and U (Sex-Unspecified).
